SAN FRANCISCO, APRIL 1-(AP)~CREW MEMBERS OF THE SCUTTLED 
GERMAN LINER COLUMBUS IN A STORY PUBLISHED TODAY IN THE SAN FRANCISCO 


CHRONICLE TOLD OF FLOODING THE SHIP WITH BENZINE TO THE EXTENT A 
PREMATURE SPARK *WOULD HAVE KILLED US ALL.” 

THE STORY, TOLD BY MEN NOW AT ANGEL ISLAND IMMIGRATION STATION 
HERE, EXPLAINED WHY TWO OF THE COLUMBUS" CREW OF 580 MEN DIED. 
THEY WERE TORCHMEN WHO "DID NOT MAKE IT® TO THE LIFEBOATS WHEN 
THE ORDER CAME TO FIRE THE BENZINE. 

THE CREW HAD BEEN INSTRUCTED WHAT TO DO SHOULD THE SCUTTLING ALARM 
BE GIVEN, THE ALARM CAME DEC.i9, WHEN A BRITISH DESTROYER ORDERED 
THE COLUMBUS TO STOP, THE PAPER QUOTED ONE CREW MEMBER? 

"ALL OF US RAN TO OUR POSTS AND BEGAN POURING THOUSANDS OF 
GALLONS OF BENZINE OVER EVERY INCH OF THE TOP FIVE DECKS. 
BEFORE WE HAD FINISHED WE WERE WADING IN BENZINE, | 

"ONE SPARK WOULD HAVE KILLED US ALL, BUT WE PRAYED THERE WOULD 
BE NO SPARK, WITHIN TEN MINUTES THE SHIP WAS SOAKING IN BENZINE, 
WE POURED THE LAET FEW GALLONS OVER THE FLOOR OF THE MAIN DINING _ 
SALON AND THEN GOT INTO LIFEBOATS, WHICH HAD BEEN SWINGING IN 
READINESS FROM THEIR DAVITS FOR TWO DAYS, - , 


AT A SIGNAL, TORCHMEN LIT THE LOWER veel TWO OF THEM DID 
NOT MAKE IT BACK TO THE LIFEBOATS. THE CAPTAIN MADE SURE THE SHIP 
WAS BURNING, THREW. ‘THE LAST TORCH ONTO THE MAIN DECK AND THEN 
LOWERED HIMSELF TO HIS MOTOR BOAT. 

"IN FIVE MINUTES THE SHIP WAS AFIRE FROM END TO END,®

DELAYED BY THE ILLNESS OF HIS DAUGHTER IN RETURNING TO HIS POST WHERE 
HE IS NEEDED."

Germany.

of nerves menacing the neutral

based on a belief that the western 
Powers have too little to gain to 
justify outright invasion of Norwe- 
gian waters to halt ore shipments 
to the Reich.

British Liner, Her Future

~ Honolulu, April 4—Completing an- 
other secret dash in her voyage from 
New York, the British liner Maure- 
tania docked here at 3.15 P. M. today 
for an unannounced period to replen- 
ish stores. 

Thousands of persons, representing 
every race in Honolulu’s melting-pot 
population, watched the huge liner 
dock, but were prevented by scores 
of customs officials, police and Gov- 
ernment agents from entering the pier: 
where she was tied up. 

Coast Guardsmen kept the harbor 
clear for the giant liner until she was, 
berthed. 
| Crew members said the Mauretania 
made a fast “blacked-out” trip from | 
the Canal Zone. 

They said the liner was under sealed 
orders, and expressed the belief the 
vessl would lave in about twenty-four 
nours. Few shore leaves were being 
granted.

Chinese: Raise- Funds 
To Aid British in War 


Chungking, April 5 ().—Gen. 
Wu Te-Chen, Chinese Overseas Af- 


irs inister, announced today 
at he had raised among Chinese 
individuals a “considerable sum” 
fer the British war organization 
in Hong Kong. 
» Wu said that 60,000 Chinese dol- 
lars (approximately $5,000) of the 
sum had been contributed by the 
overnors of Yunnan, Kiangsi, 
hensi and Chekiang provinces, 
and that the Chungking Ministers 
of Publicity and Education had 
been among the donors. The total 
raised was not given. 
«The British war fund in overseas 
colonies is organized on a commu- 
nity chest basis, the proceeds go- 
ing to all phases of civilian. and 
“home front” war effort.

DOWNs

DAYS LATER THE BRITISH ADMITTED THE 208-TON TRAWLER GORSPEN HAD BEEN 
SUNK BY GERMAN PLANES. 

THE NEW KNOWN LOSSES SENT THE TOTALS FOR THE WAR TO 503 SHIPS OF 
1,678,874 TONS, 2,770 LIVES AND 1,548 PERSONS MISSING. 

BRITAIN AND FRANCE, MEANWHILE, ANNOUNCED SHIPBUILDING PROGRAMS 
DESIGNED TO REPLACE SHIPS FASTER THAN GERMANY CAN SINK THEM.

By LOUIS P. LOCHNER 
Associated Press Correspordent 
Berlin, April 8-The German Gov- 
ernient tonight played the part of an 
“Sicily cold” observer of the two latest 
dramas in the Euronean war—Allied 
mining of Scandinavian territorial 
waters and Rumanian detention of a 


fleet of barges which the Germans 
charged were laden with British dyna- 
mite to block the vital Danube water- 
way. 
It seemed to be the intention of. 


man press. 
German propaganda officials lost n 
opportunity to use these incidents id 
weld the German nation together more 
than ever, to make every German 
citizen feel the Allies are lawbreakers 


while Germany is the defender of 
international law. 


“Sabotage Attempt” 

All papers printed the version by the 
Official news agency of the “prepos- 
‘terous sabotage attempts which the 
‘English secret service tried to carry 
out on the Danube with the aid of the 
English military.” 
_ The German press gave equal play to 
‘the minelaying in Norwegian waters. 
_ Both events; according to the news 
service, Dienst aus Deutschland, “show 
that the last restraints on Allied war 
policies have been removed and even 
breaches of law and acts of force 
against neutrals for which there is 
hardly a parallel in history are ap- 
proved.” 

The entire German press joined in 
\calling this British-French policy an 
act of despair,

sea were heard about 1 P. M. and later 
several more were reported.

At Front Comes Home. 
From War Eye 


New York, April 8 (4)—The first Cae 
nadia casualty of the European war 
to arrive in New York landed todey 
from the French liner Champlain, 
minus his left eye and nearly blind in 
the right eye. He is Julien Durupt, 36, a 
Vancouver (B.C.) electrician. 

On February 12, he said, he was sent 
to the front of the Maginot Line with 
five other men to plant mines. But the 
Germans already had mined the area,’ 
and when his party started digging an 
explosion killed his five companions, 

The liner brought two other demo- 
bilized Canadians — Silviet Carricart, 
'40, a St. Pierre (Miquelon) fStrerman, 
|whom the Government felt would be 
more valuable in his vocation, and 
Louis Abgarall, 35, a St. Laurent) 
(Manitoba) Tarmer and father of nine 
children, discharged because officia 
thought he was needed more at peas.)

Thus the Skagerrak is the key 
to the Baltic. To the Germans, 
the Battle of Jutland is known as

at the western mouth of the’

sioned officers. Military service 
is compulsory for all males. 

The largest ships of the navy are. 


two 4,000-ton vessels, one 40 and —

Britain Master After Jutland. 


After Jutland the British fleet 
was undisputed master of the Ger- 
man navy, which remained bottled 
up in the Baltic, but the full fruits 
of the British victory were not 
realized until Noy. 21, 1918, when 
the greater — of ‘the German 
High Seas Fleet surrendered to 
Admiral Beatty. 

The Skagerrak is about 140 miles 
long and 70 miles broad. It is 
shallow near _the Danish shore, 
which is low and beset with sand- 
bars, but toward the steep Nor- 
wegian coast it is deep, reaching 
a maximum of 443 fathoms.

Norris Says Invasion. Seems to 
Be ‘Take What You Can.’ 


WASHINGTON, April 9 (A. P.). 
—Germany’s advance into Denmark 


“Mr. Norris described the march 
into Scandinavia as ‘‘the same old 
process—take whatever you have 
the power to take.’’ 

Senator McNary of Oregon, the 
Republican leader, declared: ‘‘The 
United States must keep calm. No 
matter how distressing the news is

Protectorate by the Reich 


In this decisive phase of war for 
existence, forced upon the Ger- 
man people by England and 
France, the Reich government can 
under no circumstances tolerate 
that Scandinavia be converted by 
the Western powers into a theater 
of war against Germany and that 
the Norwegian people be directly 
or indirectly misused for war 
against Germany. 

Germany is unwilling to stand 
by idly or take lying down such 
a realization of enemies’ plans. 
The Reich government therefore 
has, beginning today, set in mo- 


tion certain military operations 
which will lead to the occupation 
of strategic points on Norwegian 
soil. 

The Reich government thereby 
assumes protection of the King- 
dom of Norway for the duration 


of this war. It is determined from 


now on, with its instruments of 
force, to protect peace in the North | 


against every English-French at- 


tack and definitely to render it 
secure. 

: The Reich government has not 
desired this development. The 
sponsibility, therefore, Hes solely 
with England and France. ‘To be 
‘gure, both states hypocritically pro- 
‘Claim the protection of small states, 
but in reality they violate these 
in’ the hope thereby to be able to 
translate into reality their will to 
destroy Germany, as proclaimed 
more openly each day. 

German troops, therefore, enter 
Norwegian soil not in hostile spirit. 
The German supreme command 
does not interid to use the points 
occupied by German troops as op- 
erations bases for fighting Eng- 
land as long as not forced to do so 
through acts of England and 
France, 

German military operations are 
aimed at the exclusive goal of safe- 
guarding the Norse against the in- 
tended occupation of Norwegian 
strategic points by 


French forces.

LONDON, April 9—Following is 
the text of Prime Minister Cham- 
to. the. House 
of Commens.tedey on the German 


invasion of Denmark and Norway: 
The House will be aware that © 


Germany has today invaded Den- 
mark and Norway. Ever since 
the beginning of the present war 


they have attempted to dominate 
Scandinavia and to control both 
the political and economic poli- 
cies of the Scandinavian States, 
That pressure on those States 
has been steadily increasing and, 
as is now well known, she claims 
to exercise the right to dictate 
policy as she did toward Finland 
during the Finnish-Soviet war. 


The House will recall i 
the statement I t 
of that war on t t f

‘What is the o Scan- 


dinavia? The security of Finland 
has gone, but has the security of

served? On the contrary, the 
danger has been brought closer 
to those two countries until to- 


day it stands on their doorstep.” . 


After expressing sympathy with 
those States to whom I said the 
issue of the war could not be a 
matter of indifference, I con- 
cluded: 


‘‘Nothing can or will save them 


but the determination to defend | 


themselves and to join with oth- 


ers who are ready to aid them in ' Government that their invasion of 


their defense.”’ 
Says Prophecy Is Borne Out 


Some of my listeners may have 
thought these words exagger- 
ated, but now we see the fulfill- 
ment to the letter of the prophecy 
they contained. Since that date 


the situation has further devel- — 
oped, as was pointed out in a | 
statement issued by His Majesty’s | 


Government today. The German 
Government have claimed and ex- 
ercised the right to destroy neu- 
tral and particularly Scandinavian 
shipping on the seas around this 
country by all means in their 
power. But at the same time they 


have insisted on the strict observ- 
ance of the rules of neutrality 
when this would provide some ad- 
vantage to them, as it did in Nor- 
wegian waters. 

The Allies then decided that 
they could. not recognize indefi- 
nitely this state of affairs and, 
having given notice to the Nor- 
wegian Government that they re- 


served the right to take such © 


measures as might be necessary 
to redress the balance thus 
weighted against themselves, they 
laid mine fields in Norwegian 


waters so as to prevent the un- — 


hindered passage of German traf- 
fic through them, while in no way 
interfering with normal Norwe- 
gian trade. 

At no time dig the Allies con- 
template any occupation of Scan- 


dinavian territory so long as it | 


was not attacked by Germany. 


_ Any allegations by Germany to 


the contrary are pure invention 
and have no foundation in fact.

_ that they have decided to take

are press reports that Oslo and 
Kristiansund have been bombed.

Norwegian territory at various 
places.

Norway was a reprisal for the ac-

waters. This statement will, of 
course, deceive no one. So elab- 
orate an operation, involving. si- 
multaneous landings at a.number 
of ports by troops accompanied 
by naval forces, requires planning 
long in advance, and the informa-

cates that it was already planned | 


and already in operation before 
| the mines were laid in Norwegian 


waters.

While the British did not confirm 
reports that expeditionary forces 
already were en route to Norway, 
observers held that a smashing 
blow to the German fleet was a 
necessary forerunner. 

Awaiting official reports on the 
naval results, the British also kept 
a watchful eye on Belgium and the 
Netherlands. Two Belgian fishing 
trawlers gave radio reports indicat- 
ing that Britain -was clearing all | 
shipping from the North Sea, say-' 
ing they had been taken to a con- 
trol base by British ships and that 
Netherlands fishing ‘boats were 
seen there. British northeast coast 
shippers decided to hold up all 
neutral shipping to be loaded for 
Scandinavia. 

Some observers advanced a the- 
ory that Germany’s thrust into 
Scandinavia might possibly mean a 
large-scale operation against the 
Netherlands and Belgium next.

WASHINGTON, April 10 
Broad-scale plans for removing 
Americans from Norway and Den- 
mark were laid at the State Depart- 
ment today on the basis of standing 
instructions given to American diplo-|' 
matic envoys abroad before the 
European war broke out. 

Several routes for Americans wish- 
ing to leave the two countries were 
tentatively agreed upon. Among 


1. By freighter to England from 
the Norwegian Atlantic ports of 
Bergen and Trondhjem, and thence 
to America. 

2. South from Oslo to Germany, 
with the Nazis’ permission, and then 
‘on down to Italy and out from 
Genoa, where the United States 
Lines touch. This would suffice like- 
wise for Americans in Denmark. 

3. Out direct on three American 
freighters in port at Bergen. The 
freighters are being held there 
temporarily; their capacity is small. 

The State Department lists about 
1,600 Americans living in Norway 
and Denmark. Many of these, how- 
ever, are married to Norwegians 
or. Danes or have close relatives 
there and do not want to depart. 
Probably less than half would go.

able a portion of the $500,000 spe-

| BERLIN (P)—Germany’s war 
correspondents and camera men are 
soldiers on soldiers’ pay. 

They are enlisted in the army, 
navy or air force and are militarily | 


trained. They do not represent a) 
newspaper or news agency, but are 
organized into “propaganda com-|— 
panies’’ with the armed forces. 
This arrangement springs from 
the German conception that “only}| 
a soldier has the privilege of writ-|_ 
ing about military affairs, out of 
regard for truth and thorough 
work,” 
Thus German war correspondents 
usually are in the thick of action. 
They march with the infantry, go 


diers.. In a plane, submarine or 
aboard a minesweeper they are one 
of the crew because, it'is explained, 
there is “no room for civilian 
ballast” 


"Their first-hand, eyéwitness re-| 
ports are cleared through a central 
bureau'to the papers, in which they | 
generally appear labeled merely 
“Pp. K.” (Propaganda Company). 

The articles are sorted carefully 
and distributed according to the|. 
type of reading public of each + 
paper/ 

A tradition of heroism has .~ 
veloped in the war. The propagar, 
companies have suffered a ‘‘t 
total of dead and wounded”’ ii 
lation to the troops in general 
cording to Major Hans Krav, 
the High Command. Many, .- 
received the Iron Cross, Ger:, 
war decoration.

\long statement. 


The pugnacious First Lord of the Admiralty put Ger- 
man sea losses at about eighteen vessels—four of them 
cruisers—but added to Britain’s sorrow with news of the 
loss of the destroyers Glowworm and Gurkha. } 
He branded the Nazi invasion of Norway “as great a 
strategic and political error’ as Napoleon’s disastrous 
invasion of Spain in 1808.” He declared further: 1

want of this Norwegian coast now with an enormous in- 
crease in the efficiency of our blockade.”

Islands and Iceland, are being occupied by the British to

LONDON, April 11 (A. P.).—Winston Churchill, First: 


sea war by telling the House of Commons that the German, 
invasion of Norway and Denmark, “long and elaborately’ 
prepared,” was set:in motion in the last week of March, 
breaking a “strange and unnatural calm.” 

He asked the House’s forgiveness for any small errors 
in his. statement and remarked: “The Nazi Government is 
accustomed to press through all-its channgls a 
flow of rumors.” 

The First-Lord:said that for tiénths past Britain 
‘had received information o mbers of German mer- } 
ports and of numerous small 
Vessels Seing assembled. in“various Baltic ports and also in 
‘mouths Of River Elbe. 

The Netherlands,” Denmark, beorwas! and Sweden all 


were equally liable to a sudden “brutal, capricious and 


in any casé unprovoked attack,” he said. 

Churchill said which neutral would be selected as the 
victim remained inevitably a matter of speculation, but 
he asserted that the Germans “have an obvious preference 
for striking at the weak. rather than the strong.”

Sweden Mines 100-Mile Area 
STOCKHOLM, Friday, April 12 
(P)—Swedish authorities today 
nounced they were mining a 100-, 
mile stretch of their west coast to 
guard Swedish neutrality from the 
actions of British and German fleets 
in the Kattegat. The mined waters 
extend north from Varberg, half 
way down the Kattegat, to half 
way between Lysekil and Strom- 
stad, or within 30 miles of the Nor- 
egian border near Oslo. 
orwegian minutemen, some of 
em armed with nothing but shot- 
ns, rallied to the defense of the

dish border, and defeated German 
forces before Elverum. The vol- 
unteers who arrested the Kongsvin- 
ger commander had just returned 
from Finland, where they fought 
the Russians.

220 Miles In Day 

General Kaupisch said he had been 
with the German general staff fifteen 
years, had experience in the World 
War, and “I also led a whole army 
corps in the past, and now I command 
considerably more than the usual 
_ Strength of an army corps.” 

This force, Kaupisch told me, ad- 
vanced into Jutland by motor and 
armored train and covered a distance 
of 220 miles the first day. 

Kaupisch said the Gestapo (German 
secret police) had no agents in Den- 
mark, and that no enemy civilians had 
been arrested. 


Allied Diplomats To Leave 

A decision on what to do with these 
civilians, he said, will be made soon. 
Other foreigners “who behave” will 
not be molested. 

The French and British diplomatic 
missions will be allowed to depart, 
probably Saturday, it was indicated. _ 

The Danish press will not be per- 
mitted to print anything calculated 
to harm German interests, Kaupisch 
declared, and an economic commission 
from Berlin is expected shortly to 


While may Danes took the occuna- 
tion of their country imperturbably 
the war that has caught them up was 
brought home with full force by air 
raid restrictions which blacked out 
this once gay iorthern canital. 


Police called for 250 auxiliaries to 
help during the blackout. 

Evidence of the thoroughness of 
German preparations was seen in the 
sudden appearance of hundreds of 
shaded blackout street lamps similar 
to those used in Berlin. 

Many restaurants shut long before 
their usual midnight closing time be- 
cause their customers dwindled and, 
with the sale of alcohol prohibited, 
most nightspots were closed alto- 
gether.

UNDATED SCANDINAVIAN PERSONALITIES 


THREE AGED SCANDINAVIAN MONARCHS, WHO KEPT THEIR NATIONS NEUTRAL 
DURING THE VICISSITUDES OF THE WORLD WAR, NOW ARE FACE TO FACE WITH 
THE GRIM REALITIES OF WAR DESPITE CONSTANT EFFORTS TO AVOID BEING 
DRAWN INTO THE MAELSTROM. 

KING GUSTAV V OF SWEDEN, THE OLDEST OF THE TRIO, NOW NEARLY 82 


‘YEARS OLD, HAS BEEN ON THE THRONE NEARLY 33 YEARS3 KING CHRISTIAN 


NORWAY AND SWEDEN HAD BEEN DISSOLVED. 


X OF DENMARK, NEARLY 70 YEARS OLD, HAS RULED FOR 28 YEARS AND KING — 
HAAKON, VII OF ‘NORWAY, 68, HAS REIGNED 34 YEARS. ae 
CHRISTIAN AND HAAKON ARE BROTHERS, SONS OF KING FREDERICK VIII OF 
DENMARK. 
KING GUSTAV BECAME ONE OF THE MOST DEMOCRATIC MONARCHS OF EUROPE 


DURING AND AFTER THE WORLD WAR. WHEN HE WAS CROWNED KING OF SWEDEN 


GENERALS--THE RULING HOUSE OF SWEDEN WHICH WAS ESTABLISHED IN 1818, 


IN 1881 GUSTAV MARRIED PRINCESS VICTORIA OF BADEN, A GREAT GRANDDAUGHTER 


OF ONE OF THE LAST VASA KINGS, AND A COUSIN OF THE FORMER KAISER, 
WILHELM, SHE DIED IN 1930. 

KING CHRISTIAN OF DENMARK, AS WORLD WAR SOVEREIGN, ESTABLISHED 
THE POLICY WHICH KEPT HIS LITTLE COUNTRY NEUTRAL. HE MIXES FREELY 
WITH HIS SUBJECTS, WITHOUT RETINUE OR BODY GUARD. HIS TALL, SPARE 
COURTLY FIGURE, ON HORSEBACK IS A FREQUENT SIGHT AMONG THE CROWDS. 

HIS FAMILY NAME IS SONDERBORG BECK, WHEN HE ASCENDED THE THRONE, 
FOLLOWING DANISH TRADITION, HE CHOSE THE NAME OF CHRISTIAN, "FOR ALL 
DANISH KINGS ALTERNATELY BEAR THE NAME OF CHRISTIAN AND FREDERIK. 

HE IS ADMIRED BY HIS SUBJECTS AS THE FIRST DANISH PRINCE TO 


QUALIFY FULLY IN THE COUNTRY’S SCHOOLS “AND COLLEGES, POLITICALLY, 


HE REFUSED TO ENDURE ANY OF THE POMP WITH WHICH THE ASCENSION IS USUAL ME GAVE ‘WOMEN ELECTORAL RIGHTS AND. BECAME THE NATION'S FOREMOST

This was evident from the mo- 
ment when breathless telephone

“‘the Germans have crossed

It was evident when the first

dering a warning against resistance 
and their crews flooding the city 
with green leaflets announcing that 
Nazi occupation was a fact. 


Everything Taken Complacently. 
It was evident in the very lack of 


panic among the civilian popula- | 
tion. Early risers on their way to 


shops and factories did not run at 
sight of the bombers. They mere- 
ly stood and watched, shrugging 
their shoulders as if to say, ‘Well, 
here it is.’’ 

There had been no weeks of 
*‘white war,’’ no stirring of deep 
antagonism to send them running 
for cover, 

As a result, machine guns which 
appeared in Copenhagen were more 
curiosities than anything else and 
bombers overhead were things of 
speed and power rather than po- 
tential bearers of death and de- 
struction. 


The Danes as a people cannot in! 


their hearts believe that any one 
would want to drop bombs on them,

diers stand unarmed around trucks 
with Danish bystanders grouped 
around them. From the beginning, 
German officers have moved freely 
about the streets. 

Danes find consolation in the 
thought that they are not at war. 
Sorrow over what has happened 
runs deep into their pride and af- 
fection for Denmark, for their free- 
dom and independence. 

But the Danish press says, ‘‘We 
must look to the future,’’ and re- 
minds Denmark of German assur- 
ances that her territorial integrity 
and political freedom will live— 
that the Danish flag still flies over 
Denmark and that King Christian’s 
prayer still is, ‘‘God save 
mark,”’

_ LONDON, April 12 (CP).—Food 
Ministry officials, reviewing the situ- 


ation following the Nazi invasion of 
Denmark and Norway, were reported 


ready tonight to ask Canada to help } 


replenish the British larder. A well 
informed source said Britain soon 
would be looking to the dominion 
for her main supplies of bacon and 
fish and for help with supplies of 
butter and eggs. 

It is generally conceded that the 
German booty in Denmark is “pretty 
big,” but the Ministry of Food, point- - 
ing to the present ample stocks, is 
confident that when they dwindle, 


| other sources of supply will be fune- 


tioning. 

Before her seizure by Germany, 
Denmark supplied half of Britain’s 
bacon imports, a third of the eggs, 
and a quarter of the butter imports, 
as well as a good amount of oils and 
fats for manufacturing purposes. 
Norway is not yet completely shut 


fats and fish, but the probable in- 
terruption of the flow of goods 
would be inoconvenient for Britain. 

Finland and Sweden together have 
hitherto supplied about two-thirds 
of Britain’s woodpulp and pulpwood 
imports, and, although Finland stifl 


has an ice-free port in the Arctic, 
Sweden appears to be bottled up ale 
ost. entirely.

THE. HAGUE, April 12—The 
Netheflands government, concerned 
over swift-moving developments in 
Europe, disclosed today that it is 
taking steps to guard the nation 
against “dangers” from within as 


The nature of the steps was not 
specified, but observers expressed 
belief that a curb would be placed 
on the Netherlands Nazi movement, 
which is small but active. 

semi-official statement said 
that the government is well aware 
that the Netherlands is situated “in 
the storm center of Europe” and 


that it was “fully convinced of | 
dangers which might threaten in-| 
ternally.” | 

“Therefore,” the statement said, | 


|“the government must apply the. 


strongest possible security meas-— 
ures and cannot allow itself the. 
luxury of taking any risks.” 
Warnings were issued against 
discussing military matters in pub-| 
lic places and against spreading | 


rumors either thoughtlessly or with | 
malicious intent

from the Skagerrak to Norway’s

‘dreds of bombing and reconnais- 
sance planes—would bar true com- 


parison even if the present naval

area, Units of the opposed battle

involved also frowns upon any liken- 
_ing of the present, fighting to the 
- battle of. Jutland.

Since then the Battle of Jutland 


By Associated Press, 


Despite the thunder and destruction in four days of the 


nter linked with the German 


The British argue that victory was 
theirs, at least in the ultimate 
sense, since the German high seas 
fleet thereafter offered no chal- 
lenge to the British grand fleet. 
At the war’s end it surrendered— 
and was scuttled by the Germans— 
at Scapa Flow. 
But that is an argument for ex- 
perts. What of the battle itself? 
How might it have looked to a hy- 
pothetical, omnipresent observer? 
Imagine, first, the gray, half-hid- 
den silhouettes of the German 
scouting force, filing ghostlike out 
of the Jade Estuary into Helgoland 
Bight at 2 A. M. May 31, 1916, 
trailed fifty miles astern by the 
battle fleet, nearly twoscore hulk- 
ing battleships in the escort of 
cruisers and lighter craft. 
Picture the British battle fleet in 
its broad daylight rendezvous ten 
hours later, 100 miles or so from 
the advancing German fleet and 
about the same @istance off the 
Danish coast in the mouth of the 
same Skagerrak which figures in 
today’s accounts of war at sea. 


Ships Are Spread Out. 


Don’t visualize the ships stand- 
ing closely one to the other, but 
rather deployed farther than the 
eye at water level could reach, like 
football players spread upon an 
enormous field to receive the 
kickoff. 

Now place in the expanse of sea 
between the two slowly maneuver- 
ing fleets a stray merchant steam- 
ship, her funnel smoke smearing 
the horizon—wandering like a kit- 
ten into a lion’s den. 


_ has been fought many times—in the 
_controversy over who really won. 


A lookout in the wing of the Brit- 


truder.” Simultaneously a lookout 
in the opposite wing of the Ger- 
man scouting force also spots the 
merchantman and a destroyer is 
detached to investigate. 

Another instant and the rival war- 
ships have seen each other. H. M.S. 
Galatea, from which the steamship 
had been sighted, hoists a signal 
meaning ‘‘enemy in sight.’’ 

The tracery of naval maps which 
plot the superlative battle that fol- 
lowed is a thing of complexity—b 
experts for experts. 

Suffice to say that the incident: 
of the stray merchantman brought 
the fleets into combat earlier than 
would have happened otherwise and 
thus further north on the course 0°! 
the advancing German fleet. 


Inferno of Shells Begins. 


Thus started an inferno of shells, 
ranging up to 16 inchés in diameter, 
smeke screens, the rending of steel 
and. flesh, the white furrowing of 
torpedoes and crippled ships limp- . 
ing and then slowly turning on their 
sides like stricken animals to nose 
into the sea with men plummeting 
and sliding into the water in a 
frenzied clutching at life. 
First came the running battle be- 
tween advance rival battle cruisers: 
British ships forming a single line 
and bearing down on their enemy 
at 25 knots ... batteries thundering 
in increased volume as the range 
shortens. 

Then the action of advance battle- 
ships. A shell from the German 
Luetzow rips into the British Lion’s 
midship turret, killing. nearly the 
whole gun crew . .*. the Lion is 
enveloped in smoke . . . the by- 
play of cruiser and destroyer ac- 
tions a respite 

Then at it again. . . the Luetzow 
dodging torpedoes fired from two 
and one-half miles distance .. . 
destroyers, vitally wounded, limp- 
ing to the sidelines to die... 

All these things were in the 
nature of-a warm-up. The main 
action did not get underway until 
nearly dusk when Viscount Jellicoe, 
commander-in-chief of the British 
grand fleet, ordered deployment 
into an “L’’ formation to envelop 
the German line 

The Germans slip away ...« a 
re-engagement follows ., . German

for Norway—the Allied attempt to oust 
the German invaders and gain control 
of thig land of fjords and mountains— 
“WSthiered headway today. 

The first phase, the great naval battle 
which grew out of the Nazi occupa- 
tion, still continues with the Allied 


“forces at this writing recording a very 


considerable victory. 

Nothing was reported overnight to 
controvert the claim by Britain’s First 
Lord of the Admiralty, Winston 
Churchill, that England still ruled the 
‘waves. 

Nazis Must Be Ousted 

To secure the benefit of their naval 
success, however, the Anglo-French 
brotherhood, coopefating with Nor- 
wegian regular tro6ps and volunteers, 
must clear the country of German 
troops. 

That will involve the landing of Al- 
lied expeditionary forces—a heroic and 
ganguinary business. The meaning of 
control of Norway is this: 

For Germany—It would prevent the 
opening up of a new land front for 
Allied operations against Germany’s 
right flank. It would secure the con- 
“Mtinuation of iron ore supplies from 
Sweden—an absolute necessity for the 
Reich. It would be a heavy blow to 
the Reich. It would be a heavy blow 
to the efficiency of the Allied blockade. 
It would secure large food supplies 
from Scandinavia and, by the same 
token, deprive England of them. 


Meaning To Allies 

For the Allies—It would enable the 
opening up of military operations 
against Germany from the north. It 
would deprive the Reich of sorely 
needed supplies, including the"Swedish 
ore. It would tighten the strangling 
effect of the blockade immeasurably. 
Churchill yesterday said that Hitler's 
invasion of Norway “has doubled the 
efficiency of the Allied blockade.” That 
: figure sounds rather high, but the First 
| Lord didn’t explain how he arrived at 
the estimate. In any event, he perhaps 
was counting sdme of his chicks be- 
fore they are hatched, for the Allies 
| most certainly must oust the Germens 
| from Norway in order to cash in on 
theiz-naval triumph. 

Churchill also said that the Allies 
will take what they want on the Nor- 
wegian coast, as soon as the British 
fleet has reached its primary goal, that 
is, destruction of German sea power. 
They haven't waited to reach that goal, 
however, before striking against the 
invading troops. Various landing op- 
‘erations are reported as boiling up. 

Speed is the essential in the landing 
je@perations. If the Germans succeed in 


‘ jntrenching themselves it will be a 


imffiediate Allied concern therefore} 
is to prevent Nazi reinforcéments from 


reaching Norway, and at the same 
time -get expeditionary forces ashore 
at strategic ports. 


Moving Against Trondheim

points, and it is reported that the 
Allies already are operating against 
this port, whieh also is a railroad 
terminal. Germans-this morning 
claimed to have repulsed a British 
attack with planes and naval vessels 
here,, 

Apart from the actual military and 
naval effect of this great battle, there 
is bound to be a very far-réaching 


neutrals, A clear-cut victory for either 


side will raise the stock of that belli- 


gerent immensely. 

The possibility of further explosions 
continues strong. Sweden is in grave 
danger, for if,Germany can’t get re- 
inforcements into Norway in any other 
way, there is small doubt that she will 
attempt to put them through Sweden. 


Holland Prepared 

Holland#hag prepared for eventuali- 
ties, for she might easily be one of the 
next to be taken over by Nazidom in 
order to provide air and submarine 
bases for operations against England. 
The Balkans, especially Rumania, 
fear invasion—an anxiety which is 
fully justified. 

If the war flames sweep the Balkans.

of non-belligerency very hard to main- 
tain. Any day now he may discover 
himself: in the position of having to 
decide which side he is going to join.

Kan states which haven’t already in- 
dicated their position. Turkey, of

THE HAGUE, April 13 (4).—The 
Netherlands faced tonight its most 
critical period since the outbreak 
of the European war—with its 
armed forces alert to strike back at 
any invasion, new strategic areas 
under martial law and the govern-} 
ment reiterating its vow to main-| 
tain a policy of complete independ- 


ence despite APR t) qrr 
ring powers. 
Belgium, too, invoked new defen- 
Sive measures today, posting mili- 
tary guards at all public properties 
—radio stations, ministries and air-|' 
dromes. The guards were described 
officially as precautionary, “because 


of the general tension.” Additional) 
army leaves were banned. There’ 


has been a constant rising of ten-|. 


sion in Brussels in the last few days, 
and the Belgian franc has been fall- 
ing slowly.

was given control over additional 
zones in the southeastern Province

first defense lines are located, and 


in northern and eastern provinces. ,-

THE NATION'S BIRTHDAY GIFT TO THE FUEHRER: EVERY CITIZEN, RICH OR

INDIVIDUALS THEMSELVES TO SEND SUCH GIFTS AS THEY MIGHT DEEM 
PROPER TO SHOW THEIR LOVE FOR THEIR FUEHRER. 

BRONZE, COPPER NICKEL, TIN, BRASS==THESE ARE THE METALS 
NEEDED FOR CONDUCTING ACTIVE WARFARE. HITLER SPOKESMEN HAVE STATED. 
AGAIN AND AGAIN THAT ARMS WOULD BE SPEAKING DURING THE WEEKS TO 
CONE, AND THAT ALL PEACE TALK WAS JUST SO MUCH NONSENSE,

FIRST BIRTHDAY WILL BEAR ELOQUENT TESTIMONY OF THE DETERMINATION OF 
THE NAZI REGIME TO JUSTIFY DER FUEHRER"S HOPE, EXPRESSED IN HIS -NEW 
YEAR*#S MESSAGE "MAY THE YEAR 1940 BRING THE DECISION-=IT WILL MEAN 
OUR VICTORY, COME WHAT MAY."

Demands Listed By Norway 

The demands listed were: 

1. A proclamation to. be made to | 
the people and the army ordering | 
no opposition to Germany. 

2. The army to be ordered to make 
contact with the advancing Ger- 
mans and give them loyal col- 
laboration. The army to be al- 
lowed to keep its weapons if its 
conduct permitted. All military | 


buildings to hoist a white flag | 


beside the Norwegian flag as a | 
sign of their collaboration. 


3. The military buildings needed 


by Germany to secure Norway | 


against foreign enemies to be de- 


livered undamaged, especially | 


coastal fortresses. 


mine fields to be delivered to 
Germany.

of occupation. .

tained at Germany’s disposition.

to foreign ports and no air serv- 
ice to be permitted, with the 
understanding that maritime 
commerce would be permitted 
later to German and neutral

to obey German orders.

[By the Associated Press] 
April 15—Dr, Karl 


of today that twenty 
days before Germany moved against 
Poland Adolf Hitler declared he “had 


no such scruples as Wilhelm II” and| 


that he “would fight without mercy 
up to the extreme limits.” 
In a report to the League Council 


at Obersalzburg, August 11, Dr. 
Burckhardt, League High Commis- 
sioner for Danzig, portrayed the Nazi 
chieftain as alternately boasting of 
Germany’s armed might and insisting 
on his desire for peace. 

Hitler said that, although the Ger- 
man army leaders were eautious dur- 
ing the Czecho-Slovak crisis in 1938, 
he had to restrain them in the Polish 
crisis. 

Discussions Held Foolish 

Burckhardt, who had gone to Hitler 
in an attempt to arbitrate the prob- 
lem of Danzig, which was absorbed by 
Germany after the outbreak of the 
war last September, reported the 
Chancellor told him “eternal discus- 
sions on war were folly and that they 
brought nations to a state of mad- 
ness.” 

The report quoted Hitler as saying 
of Russia that “Germany knew them 


“He wished to put out two other 
firebrands—Memel and Danzig—but 


‘took a step, he found England and

| New Nazi Troops Coming In. 


New German troops and supplies 
are arriving daily. German ships 
are unloading food for the troops. 

German soldiers are permitted to 
use reichsmarks at the rate of one 
mark to 1.66 kroner. 

The German occupation proceeds 
quickly and systematically. There 
is direct railway communication 
tonight to the Kristiansand district 
‘in the south and to Kornsjo at the 
Swedish border in the southeast. 

The occupation has been extended 
to Drammen, Kongsberg, Honefoss, 
Eidsvoll, Elverum, Askim, Sarps- 
borg, Fredrikstad, Halden and 
Kornsjo. 

There is no direct censorship for 
newspapers, except for what the 
situation and“common sense direct. 
There are no restrictions against 
listening to radio broadcasts from 
abroad. 

‘Some motion picture theaters are 
open. Food and milk are available. 
Church meetings and services are 
-held as usual. There is a complete 
blackout in the Oslo district, but 
there is no restriction on the méve- 
ments of citizens in the streets.

THE NETHERLANDS INDIES ARE VERY IMPORTANT IN THE INTERNATIONAL 
RELATIONSHIPS OF THE WHOLE PACIFIC OCEAN. THE ISLANDS THEMSELVES 
EXTEND FOR A DISTANCE OF APPROXIMATELY THREE THOUSAND TWO HUNDRED 
MILES EAST AND WEST ASTRIDE OF THE EQUATOR, FROM THE INDIAN OCEAN 
ON THE WEST FAR INTO THE PACIFIC OCEAN ON THE EAST. THEY ARE 
ALSO AN IMPORTANT FAVTOR IN THE COMMERCE OF THE WHOLE WORLD. 
EY PRODUCE CONSIDERABLE PORTIONS OF THE WORLD'S SUPPLIES OF IMPORTANT 
ESSENTIAL COMMODITIES SUCH AS RUBBER, TIN, QUININE, COPRA, 
ET CETERA, MANY COUNTRIES, INCLUDING THE UNITED STATES, 
DEPEND SUBSTANTIALLY UPON THEM FOR SOME OF THESE COMMODITIES. 


INTERVENTION IN THE DOMESTIC AFFAIRS OF THE NETHERLANDS INDIES OR 


ANY ALTERATION OF THEIR STATUS QUO BY OTHER THAN PEACEFUL 


PROCESSES WOULD BE PREJUDICIAL TO THE CAUSE OF

By LOUIS P. LOCHNER 
Associated Press Correspondent 


Berlin, April 17—German destroyer 
a the Norwegian port 
of Narvik, having shot all their muni- 
tions in two battles with British ships 
at that far-north ore shipping town, 
are ready to continue the fight on land, 
a German naval officer who was 
wounded in the first engagement de- 
clared today. 

The officer, Commander Heinrich 
Gerlash, 33, an Admiralty staff officer 
assigned to Commodore Fritz Bonte, 
chief of the destroyer flotilla in north- 
ern Norwegian waters, told his story 
shortly before he was decorated with 
the Iron Cross first class by Grand 
Admiral Erich Raeder, head of the 
German navy. 

Commander Gerlach was flown to 
Berlin from Narvik for hospitaliza- 


jtion for injuries suffered when a | 


British “shell” scored a direct hit on 
his ship in the first battle of Narvik 
April 10. He was still in Narvik when 
Commodore Bonte was killed by an- 
other direct hit in the second battle 
April 13. 

“Narvik city, harbor and _ entire |: 
hinterland up to tthe Swedish border |,

Narvik by airplane,” he said.

| Narvik, but did assert his turn for 
' transport home came after the English 
had “for days already been claiming | 
the capture of Narvik.”

{By the Associated Press] 
London, Thursday, April 18—Numer- 
ous German bombers were reported 
early today to have attacked shipping 
in the Downs, Britain’s big English 
Channel contraband control point. 
The sound of heavy firing and the 
roar of intercepting airplanes was 
heard along the southeast coast. 
The London News Chronicle said 
the firing resulted from an attack on 
the Downs, where neutral ships are 
taken for examination of their cargoes.

BERLIN, April 19 (A. P.). 


Therefore, the diplomats and their 
families*departed at 5 P. M. by spe- 
cial train and were given until mid- 
night to get out of Germany. A 
member of the German Foreign Of- 
fice Protocol Staff accompanied 
them. 
The Norwegians left so hurriedly 
that the problem of liquidating 
their households was left to the 
Swedish Legation. They planned to 
travel by way of Hamburg, Flens- 
burg and Frederica to Copenhagen 
where they hoped to catch a ferry 
for Norway.

operations on land 
‘and sea and in the air tonight as she

Keeps Arabs on 
Side of Britain 


Scar-Faced Abou Heineik 
(Maj. Glubb) Respected 


APR 
LO orrespondéh if The 


Associated Press).—German agents” 
are reported to be dangling gold and 
promises before Arab tribal leaders. 
south of the Transjordan border in 
attempts to stir up desert revolt. 

The game they are trying is the 
one Lawrence of Arabia played and 
won for England in the last war. 
The immediate prize is the pipeline 
from Iraq to Haifa—the chief oil 


‘|supply within the Allied countries. 


Besides this thousand miles of. 
iron tubing is the juicy ,plum of 
Moslem support. Revolt jn*the Ma- 
hometan world of 250,000,000 stretch- 


ing from India to the Atlantic at 
Morocco could break the British and 


'|French empires of the Near East. 


Britons are confident they will 


‘}thwart any German-backed revolt. 
because they hold a Near Eastern 
'‘}trump—an Englishman with a scar 


on his chin and a host of Bedouin 


listed as Maj. John Glubp, organ- 
izer of the tesert Vitra of the Arab 


jordan tribesmen call him Abo 
Heineik—the man with the jaw. 

e has stepped into Lawrence's 
shoes to keep the Arabs on Britain’s 
side. This time it is Britain that is 
on the defensive in the Near East. 
But the British feel that their posi- 
tion is far stronger than was that 
of the Turks, against whom Law- 
rence stirred the Arabs to rebellion! 


twenty-five years ago. 


No effort has been spared to con- 


| solidate the influence over Mahome- 


tan countries which came to Britain 
and France with the breakup of the 
old Turkish Empire at the end of 
the last war. 

Now a treaty with her former 
enemy, Turkey, and concessions to 
Arabs in Palestine have. given 
Britain a strong political hand. 
| Australian, New Zealand. ¥tench 


British, Indian, Turkish and Egyp- 


tian troops are on guard along the; 4 
‘during the “peace months” of Janu-| 


coasts, while men such as Maj. 
Glubb have closed desert back doors 
against tribal uprising. 

The scar on his chin came from 
a wound in the last war. They call 
-him a great fighter—a reputation 


he won when he co-ordinated Irak ~ 


and Bedouin tribes in 1924 and lec 
them against mara ding bands from 
Saudi Arabia to the south. 

Backing him up was Emir Ab- 
dullah Bin Hussein, now ruler ol 
Transjordan and onetime comrade 
of Lawrence. Abdullah’s brother 
Feisal was lLawrence’s Arabian 
right-hand man. 

It is an honor for an Arab to belong 
to the camel-mvuunted desert patrol. 
They wear a bright galabieh with 
long white sleeves, a scarlet cloak 
and a gay (shawl) and agal (rope 
crown) on their heads. 

The British major is quiet, studi- 
ous, slender, stoop shouldered. - He 
speaks Arabic better than Law- 
rence did. He has the same insight 
into Arab character.

ONE HALF MONTHS OF WAR WITH SOVIET RUSSIA. THEY ARE FINLAND'S LOSSES

THE INTENSE WAR FOOTING IN EFFECT HERE DURING THE WAR» 

TEN PERCENT OF THE ENTIRE POPULATION WAS UNDER ARMS AND ALMOST AS

OF MAINTAINING SUCH A MILITARY ORGANIZATION WAS ASTRONOMICAL, TO SAY

AND 20,000 OR 30,000 ORPHANS.® 

THE BARE STATEMENT THAT FINLAND LOST 10 PERCENT OF HER TERRITORY

ONE GREAT BLOW TO FINNISH ECONOMY WILL BE THE LOSS OF THE LOWER 
PART OF THE INTERNAL WATER TRANSPORTATION SYSTEM. THE RUSSIANS NOW 
HAVE POSSESSION OF THE LOWER SECTION OF THE SAIMA CANAL AND THE GREAT

SO MUCH FOR THE COST OF THE WAR. WHAT ABOUT THE FUTURE OF 


FINLAND AND WHAT ARE THE PROBLEMS SHE FACES? | 
FINLAND IS FAR FROM A BEATEN NATION! NO CONQUERED STATE WOULD 


DARE TO CRITICIZE HER CONQUEROR AS FINNISH LEADERS HAVE 


CRITICIZED RUSSIA, NOR TO DECLARE OPENLY THE INTENTION TO STRENGTHEN 
HER DEFENSES AGAINST POSSIBLE THREATS OF THE FUTURE. 


THE WHOLE ATTITUDE BOTH OF THE PEOPLE AND THE GOVERNMENT IS ONE OF 
CONFIDENCE AND DETERMINATION. 


IN THESE WORDS ARE STATED BRIEFLY FINLAND'S TWO GREAT PROBLEMS: 
i--RECONSTRUCTION OF HER DEVASTATED AREAS AND THE CARE FOR 
THE THOUSANDS OF HOMELESS. APR 1940 


2-“BUILDING STRONG DEFENSES AGAINST FUTURE ATTACK.

ATION IN THE HEAVY SACRIFICES WHICH THE NATION HAS BEEN MAKING SINCE

RECONSTRUCTION PLANS ARE STILL IN THE PRELIMINARY STAGE. THE FIRST 
TASK WAS THE EMERGENCY JOB OF EVACUATING THE AREAS CEDED TO RUSSIA AND 
FINDING TEMPORARY SHELTERS==AS WELL AS FOOD AND CLOTHING==FOR THE 
REFUGEES, 


THE QUESTION OF PERMANENT HOMES AND MEANS OF LIVLIHOOD FOR THESE 


THOUSANDS IS ONE THAT WILL TAKE TIME. MANY COMMUNITIES, HOWEVER, HAVE 


CONTRIBUTED LAND AND ADVANCED OTHER PLANS TO HELP SOLVE THE 


PROBLEM. 
INDUSTRIAL CENTERS LIKE HELSINKI ARE EXPECTED TO ABSORB MANY OF 


THE PEOPLE FROM CITIES IN THE CEDED AREAS. A PLAN ALREADY HAS BEEN 
PUT FORWARD FOR THE DEVELOPMENT OF DEGEROE, A SECTION OF HELSINKI 
ALONG THE COAST. THE PLANS CALL FOR IMPROVEMENT 
OF THE HARBOR AND EXTENSION OF THE RAILROAD TO DEGEROE. EFFORTS 
ALSO ARE BEING MADE TO ARRANGE FOR LOW PRICED LAND PLOTS TO ENCOURAGE 
BUILDING OF RESIDENCES AND NEW INDUSTRIES.

[By the Associated Press] 

London, Tuesday, April 23—A dispatch from 
the Norwegian-Swedish frontier by Reuters said to- 
day that German destroyers from Trondheim had 
landed troops north of Trondheim with the object of 
attacking British forces from the rear, but that they 
had been driven off by British troops. 


The dispatch said fierce fighting now is going 
on between German and British troops at Stikle- 


stad, north of Trondheim, between Steinkjer and 
Vardalsora.

After studying Great 8 
new war budget, statisticians 
estimated. today that increased 
taxes on beer, tobacco and 
postage and telephone calis 
would cost the average man a 


shilling and seven pence, or 
about 40 cents, a week. 

This is based on the estimate 
that the average Briton buys 
two and half pints of beer a 
week, smokes seventy cigarettes, 
posts five letters and makes 
seven telephone calls.

Three Battlefronts. 


Norway now is carved into three 
battlefronts—the Oslo ‘‘gateway’’ in 
the southeast, Trondheim on ‘the 
Atlantic coast and Narvik in the 
far north. 

The first two are closely related. 

The Germans hold Trondheim, but 
Allied forces have landed at An- 
dalsnes, about 100 miles to the 
south, and Namsos, about the same 


being confronted with steadily in- 
creasing raids by small Norwegian 
patrols, including expert skiers 
who are making the most of re-) 
maining snows. 

Emulating the Finns in sudden 
attacks at strategic points, the Nor- 
wegians are beginning to dart in) 
wherever possible dynamite | 
bridges and roads. 

Though pftneipal fighting focused 
on the Trondheim Fjord area, Ger- 
man warplanes also ranged the 
length of east central Norway 
while their land forces pressed 
further the Nazi occupation.

between the two Allied columns.|

toward Oslo, bisecting Norway.
